topic.name: Sketching a Function From the Graph of its Derivative

question.text: If $f'(x)=|x-1|$ and $f(2)=3,$ which of the following could be the graph of a continuous function $y=f(x)?$
question.explanation:
The graph of $y=f'(x)$ is the following:

Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there is one critical point:

$\qquad$ $x=1$

Also, we have the following:

  • If $f'(x) > 0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

  • If $f'(x) < 0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

$x$ $(-\infty,1)$ $1$ $(1,\infty)$
$f'$ $+$ $0$ $+$
$f$ $\nearrow$ $\textrm{no extr.}$ $\nearrow$

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

  • First, we draw the critical point. Consider the vertical line $x=1.$

    • Since we are told that $f(2)=3,$ we can draw that point on the graph.

    • Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(1,2),$ the point at $x=1$ must be lower than the point at $x=2.$

    So, we draw it as follows:

  • Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

    • Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-\infty,1)$ and is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(1,\infty)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left of $x=1$ and goes up to the right of $x=1.$

    • Furthermore, since $f'(x)$ is decreasing to the left of $x =1$, we must have $f''(x) < 0$, and, since it is increasing to the right of $x = 1$, we must have $f''(x) > 0.$ So, $x = 1$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave down to concave up.

    So, we can draw as follows:

  • Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

question.text: The graph of $y=f'(x),$ the derivative of $f(x),$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.explanation:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points:

$\qquad$ $x=-2\quad$ and $\quad x=2$

Also, we have the following:

  • If $f'(x) > 0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

  • If $f'(x) < 0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.

$x$ $(-\infty,-2)$ $-2$ $(-2,2)$ $2$ $(2,\infty)$
$f'$ $+$ $0$ $-$ $0$ $+$
$f$ $\nearrow $ $\textrm{max}$ $\searrow$ $\textrm{min}$ $\nearrow $

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

  • First, we draw the critical points. We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical lines $x=-2$ and $x=2.$ Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-2,2),$ the point at $x=-2$ must be higher than the point at $x=2,$ as shown below.

  • Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

    • Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-\infty,-2)$ and is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-2,2)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=-2.$

    • Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-2,2)$ and is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(2,\infty)$, the graph of $y=f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=2.$

  • Finally, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

Note: The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$

question.text: The graph of $y=f'(x)$, the derivative of a continuous function $y=f(x)$, is given above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y=f(x)?$
question.explanation:
Recall that critical points of $y=f(x)$ occur when $f'(x)=0$ or $f'(x)$ does not exist. In our case, there are two critical points:

$\qquad$ $x=-1\quad$ and $\quad x=1$

Also, we have the following:

  • If $f'(x) > 0$ then $f(x)$ is increasing.

  • If $f'(x) < 0$ then $f(x)$ is decreasing.

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below.


$x$ $(-\infty,-1)$ $-1$ $(-1,1)$ $1$ $(1,\infty)$
$f'$ $-$ $0$ $+$ $0$ $-$
$f$ $\searrow $ $\textrm{min}$ $\nearrow$ $\textrm{max}$ $\searrow$

Let's now sketch the graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

  • First, we draw the critical points. Consider the vertical lines $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

    • We choose an arbitrary point on the vertical line $x=1.$

    • Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-1,1),$ the point at $x=-1$ must be lower than the point at $x=1.$

    So, we draw it as follows:

  • Next, we consider the behavior of $y=f(x)$ in the neighborhood of the critical points:

    • Since $f(x)$ is decreasing $\searrow$ on $(-\infty,-1)$ and increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-1,1)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes up to the left and to the right of $x=-1.$

    • Since $f(x)$ is increasing $\nearrow$ on $(-1,1)$ and decreasing $\searrow$ on $(1,\infty)$, the graph of $f(x)$ goes down to the left and to the right of $x=1.$

    • Furthermore, since $f'(x)$ is increasing to the left of $x = 0$, we must have $f''(x) > 0$, and, since it is decreasing to the right of $x = 0$, we must have $f''(x) < 0.$ So, $x =0$ is an inflection point at which the curve $y=f(x)$ changes from concave up to concave down.

  • Finally, since we are told that our graph must be continuous, by connecting and extending the existing parts with a smooth curve, we obtain a possible graph of $y=f(x)\mathbin{:}$

Note: The graph we obtained is not the only possible one. Any similar graph that's shifted vertically up or down could also be considered a possible $y=f(x).$
